references.sentence: In this section, we ﬁrst discuss the proper reset timing, study the concept of using a bottom-level envelope signal to create reset on chip, and ﬁnally analyze the detail reset creation circuit. 1) Reset Timing: To create a reset on-chip based only on the incoming burst signal, the appropriate timing for reset creation is shown in Fig. 7(a) and can be described as follows. • After the end of a burst, during guard time, an envelope detector detects the absence of the signal and via a logic circuit turns reset on. • Reset is kept on during the guard time. • At the beginning of a new burst, the envelope detector detects the presence of the signal and via a logic circuit turns reset off. • Reset is kept off until the end of the burst, and then reset is turned on again during the next guard time.
As shown in Fig. 7(a), the ﬁrst portion of burst data—the dummy pattern—lies in the reset-on period and, therefore, is distorted.

After a burst, the reset creation circuit needs some time to detect the signal’s absence so the reset is turned on with some delay compared to the actual burst period. 2) Bottom-Level Envelope and Reset Creation: Fig. 7(b) depicts output waveforms and its bottom-level envelope (BLE).
Ideally, during guard time when no signal comes into the receiver, the voltages at the two receiver outputs become equal to the dc level, as shown in Fig. 7(b).

By comparing this envelope signal to a reference voltage located between the dc level and the negative peak of output swing [Fig. 7(b)], with some additional logic circuits, reset is turned on during guard time and turned off during the burst period. 3) Circuit Implementation: The reset creation circuit block diagram is shown in Fig. 8.
Recall in Fig. 7(b) the reset creation concept: in a real case, output voltages vary arbitrarily after a burst, depending on the burst input power level.
Fig. 7.
In Fig. 7(b), after a burst, a BLE signal of an output rises up , thereby turning reset on.
